items.name: Barangays, Rajahnates & Sultanates
items.description: The Laguna Copperplate Inscription, dated 900 CE, is the oldest known written document from the islands and records a debt settlement among local elites. Communities were organised in barangays led by datus, and larger trading polities such as Tondo, Cebu, and Butuan traded with China and Southeast Asia. Islam spread in the south, where the Sultanate of Sulu (15th century) and the Sultanate of Maguindanao rose.

items.name: Tondo, Maynila, Namayan & Caboloan
items.description: The Laguna Copperplate Inscription of 900 names Tundun (Tondo) on the north bank of the Pasig delta. Graves under the Santa Ana church at Namayan (Sapa), upriver, hold Chinese and Southeast Asian trade wares of the 12th to 15th centuries. Envoys from Pangasinan — Caboloan on the Agno delta — brought tribute to the Ming court in 1403–1405. Maynila, on the south bank, was by Bruneian tradition founded as a Bornean trading colony about 1500. These were towns of allied barangays under datus, lakans and rajahs, not territorial kingdoms. Martín de Goiti attacked Maynila in 1570; Legazpi declared Spanish Manila on its site on 24 June 1571, Lakandula of Tondo made peace, and Juan de Salcedo conquered Pangasinan in 1572.

periods.name: Spanish conquest of Manila Bay and Pangasinan

items.name: Butuan, Cebu & the Visayan Ports
items.description: Butuan, a gold-trading port on the Agusan River in north-eastern Mindanao, sent its first tributary mission to the Song court on 17 March 1001, and more in 1003 and 1011; the balangay plank boats excavated there show its seafaring. Cebu (Sugbu) was a long seaside port-kingdom on the strait facing Mactan, probably the 'Suwu' of Zhao Rugua's Zhufan Zhi (1225). In 1521 Magellan's fleet met Rajah Siagu of Butuan and Rajah Kolambu at Limasawa, where the first Mass was said on 31 March, and Rajah Humabon of Cebu, who was baptised; on 27 April Lapulapu of Mactan defeated and killed Magellan. Legazpi took Cebu from Rajah Tupas in 1565.

items.name: Sulu, Maguindanao, Buayan & Lanao
items.description: Islam reached the southern islands through traders and preachers from the 14th century. Sharif ul-Hashim founded the Sultanate of Sulu at Buansa on Jolo in 1405 or 1457; it ruled the Sulu Archipelago and, from 1658 or 1704, north-east Borneo. Shariff Kabungsuwan founded Maguindanao's sultanate in the Cotabato basin in the early 1500s, and under Sultan Kudarat (r. c. 1619–1671) it was the strongest power in Mindanao. Buayan, upriver, was its rival; the Maranao lords of Lake Lanao seceded from Maguindanao in 1616 and governed by council. The sultanates resisted Spain for three centuries; Sulu gave up temporal power to the United States in 1915.

items.name: Spanish Philippines
items.description: Ferdinand Magellan's expedition arrived in 1521, and Magellan was killed at Mactan by forces under Lapulapu. Miguel López de Legazpi began lasting Spanish colonisation in 1565 and made Manila the capital in 1571. For 250 years the Manila galleons carried Asian goods to Acapulco in exchange for American silver. Catholicism became the majority faith. In the late 19th century reformers such as José Rizal pressed for change; his execution in 1896 helped fuel the Katipunan-led revolution.

items.name: Spanish–Moro Wars
items.description: For three centuries Spain fought the sultanates of Sulu and Mindanao, while Moro fleets raided the Visayas and Luzon for captives. Buayan and Maguindanao beat back a Spanish expedition in 1596. Governor-General Sebastián Hurtado de Corcuera built Fort San José at Zamboanga (1635), stormed Kudarat's fort at Lamitan (1637), took Jolo (1638) and sent an expedition to Lake Lanao (1639), but Spain left Jolo in 1646 and abandoned Zamboanga in 1663 against the threat of Koxinga, returning only in 1718 (Fort Pilar). Steam gunboats turned the tide in the 19th century: Spain took Jolo in 1876 and reached Marawi in 1895.

sources.title: Saleeby, The History of Sulu (Manila, 1908) — Project Gutenberg

items.name: Revolts against Spain: Dagohoy to Biak-na-Bato
items.description: Francisco Dagohoy's revolt in Bohol (1744–1829), the longest in Philippine history, made northern Bohol a free territory for 85 years. When Britain occupied Manila and Cavite (October 1762 – April 1764), Diego Silang led an Ilocano revolt until he was assassinated on 28 May 1763; his widow Gabriela carried it on until she was hanged that September. The Cavite mutiny of January 1872 and the execution of the priests Gomez, Burgos and Zamora (Gomburza) radicalised a generation of reformers. Andrés Bonifacio founded the Katipunan in Tondo on 7 July 1892 and launched the Revolution in August 1896; under Emilio Aguinaldo the rebels signed the constitution of the Republic of Biak-na-Bato on 1 November 1897, then made a truce with Spain in December 1897.

items.name: First Republic & Philippine–American War
items.description: Emilio Aguinaldo declared independence on 12 June 1898, but Spain ceded the islands to the United States in the Treaty of Paris that December. The Malolos (First Philippine) Republic was proclaimed in January 1899, and war with the United States broke out a month later. The US declared the war over in 1902, though resistance continued for years. Civilian deaths from fighting, famine, and disease are estimated in the hundreds of thousands, and the figures remain debated.

sources.title: Office of the Historian — The Philippine-American War, 1899–1902

items.name: American Colony, Commonwealth & War
items.description: American rule introduced English-language public schooling and an elected legislature while keeping ultimate control in Washington. The 1935 Commonwealth under President Manuel Quezon set a path to independence. Japan invaded in December 1941; the Bataan Death March of 1942 and the destruction of Manila in 1945 were among the war's worst episodes in the islands. The Philippines became independent on 4 July 1946.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Japanese occupation of the Philippines

items.name: Third Republic & Marcos Era
items.description: The young republic faced the Hukbalahap rebellion and close ties to the United States. Ferdinand Marcos, elected in 1965, declared martial law in September 1972 and ruled by decree; it was formally lifted in 1981. The assassination of opposition leader Benigno Aquino Jr. in 1983 galvanised resistance, and the peaceful People Power Revolution on EDSA in February 1986 drove Marcos from power.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Martial law under Ferdinand Marcos

items.name: Bangsamoro: from the MNLF to BARMM
items.description: The killing of Moro recruits on Corregidor in March 1968 (the Jabidah massacre) and decades of settlement of Mindanao from the north fed a Moro independence movement. Nur Misuari founded the Moro National Liberation Front a month after martial law, in October 1972; the Tripoli Agreement (23 December 1976) promised autonomy, and the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao was created in 1989. The MNLF made peace in 1996; the breakaway Moro Islamic Liberation Front signed the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro in 2014. In 2017 ISIS-linked fighters besieged Marawi for five months. After the Bangsamoro Organic Law (2018) and the plebiscite of January–February 2019, the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) replaced the ARMM, with its seat at Cotabato City; in 2024 the Supreme Court ruled Sulu out of the region.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro

items.name: Fifth Republic
items.description: Corazon Aquino's presidency produced the 1987 constitution. The 1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo was one of the largest of the 20th century, and US forces left Subic Bay in 1992. A second popular uprising (EDSA II) removed Joseph Estrada in 2001. In 2016 an international arbitral tribunal ruled for the Philippines against China's South China Sea claims, and Rodrigo Duterte's drug war (2016–2022) drew wide criticism over extrajudicial killings. The Bangsamoro autonomous region was created in 2019 after a long peace process.

sources.title: PCA — The South China Sea Arbitration
